name: AI for Multilingual Learners
objectives: Given a grade-level passage, adapt the text with AI to lower the language load while keeping the grade-level ideas, passing the same-questions test
For one lesson's key words, make a bilingual glossary of 8 to 10 words in a home language your school serves, with cognates marked, checked by a qualified speaker, with every correction recorded

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Language supports that keep the learning high
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Adapt a text for language load without lowering the grade-level ideas.
This lesson builds toward: Given a grade-level passage, you will adapt the text with AI to lower the language load while keeping the grade-level ideas, passing the same-questions test.
Multilingual learners can think at grade level while still learning English. The goal of a support is to lower the language load, not the thinking. That means keeping the key concepts, vocabulary and questions, while adding clarity: shorter sentences, headings, visuals, key terms in bold with definitions.
Prompt: "Adapt this 7th-grade science passage for students learning English at an intermediate level. Keep every key concept and these academic words: [list]. Use shorter sentences and headings, bold the academic words and define each in simple English. Do not remove ideas."
Check the adapted text against the original for accuracy. A good test: could a student who reads the adapted text answer the same main questions as a student who read the original?
Step by step:
- List the key concepts and academic words.
- Ask AI to adapt for language level, keeping both.
- Add headings, visuals and bolded terms with definitions.
- Check accuracy against the original.
- Test: same main questions answerable?
Words to know:
- Multilingual learner: a student learning in more than one language, often still developing English.
- Language load: how hard the language of a text is, separate from how hard the ideas are.
- Academic vocabulary: words used in school subjects, like analyze, evidence or photosynthesis.
Try it now: Adapt one grade-level passage with AI for an intermediate English level, keeping all key concepts. Check it with the same-questions test.
You can now adapt texts for multilingual learners without lowering the grade-level ideas.

options: How hard the language is, separate from the ideas
How many pages a text has
How many students speak a language
check.why: Lowering language load makes the text easier to read without lowering the ideas.

check.q: AI's adapted passage drops a key concept to make it shorter. What would you do?
options: Give multilingual learners an easier topic
Put the concept back and check with the same-questions test
Ask students to skip that part
check.why: Adapted texts keep key concepts so students learn at grade level.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Bilingual glossaries and cognates
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Make a checked bilingual glossary for a lesson's key words.
This lesson builds toward: For one lesson's key words, you will make a bilingual glossary of 8 to 10 words in a home language your school serves, with cognates marked, checked by a qualified speaker, with every correction recorded.
A bilingual glossary gives each key word in English, a simple definition, the word in the student's home language, and an example sentence. AI can draft one quickly in many languages: "Make a glossary table of these 10 words for 5th-grade science: English word, simple definition, Spanish translation, example sentence in English."
Ask AI to mark cognates (words that look and mean the same in both languages, like "animal" and "animal" or "information" and "información") and false friends (words that look alike but mean different things). Cognates are a strength students bring.
AI translations of single words can pick the wrong meaning for your subject (for example, a math or science term with an everyday meaning). Have a qualified speaker, such as a bilingual teacher or district translator, check the glossary before students use it.
Step by step:
- List 8-10 key words.
- Ask for a table: word, definition, home-language word, example.
- Ask AI to mark cognates and false friends.
- Have a qualified speaker check it.
- Share it with students before the lesson.
Words to know:
- Bilingual glossary: a list of key words with meanings in two languages.
- Cognate: a word that looks and means about the same in two languages.
- False friend: a word that looks similar in two languages but means something different.
Try it now: Make a bilingual glossary of 8 to 10 words for one lesson in a home language your school serves, with cognates marked. Ask a qualified speaker to check it and record any corrections.
You can now create bilingual glossaries that build on students' home languages.

options: A cognate that means the same in two languages
A word that looks similar in two languages but means something different
A friend who translates for you
check.why: False friends look like cognates but mislead, so they need marking.

check.q: AI translated a science word with its everyday meaning instead of its subject meaning. What do you do?
options: Remove the word from the glossary
Ask AI for a longer definition
Have a qualified speaker correct it and record the correction
check.why: AI single-word translations may pick the wrong meaning for your subject.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Sentence frames by proficiency level
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write sentence frames at three levels for a speaking or writing task.
This lesson builds toward: Given a lesson's main speaking or writing task, you will write sentence frames at three proficiency levels with a word bank, with every level asking for the same thinking.
Sentence frames give students the structure of academic language so they can focus on ideas. For the same task, students at different English levels need different support. Example task: explain whether a claim is supported by evidence.
Ask AI for three levels. Beginning: short frames with a word bank ("The claim is ___. The evidence is ___."). Intermediate: frames with connecting words ("The claim is supported because ___. However, ___."). Advanced: open starters and academic connectors ("Although the evidence suggests ___, it does not fully account for ___.").
Post all three levels so students can choose and move up. Check that every level asks for the same thinking. Your district's English language development standards and your ELD colleagues can help you match frames to proficiency levels.
Step by step:
- Name the speaking or writing task.
- Ask for frames at beginning, intermediate and advanced levels.
- Add a word bank at the beginning level.
- Check every level asks for the same thinking.
- Post all three; let students move up.
Words to know:
- Sentence frame: a sentence with blanks that shows the structure of a response.
- Proficiency level: how far a student has developed in English.
- Connector: a word that links ideas, like because, however or although.
Try it now: Pick a speaking or writing task from an upcoming lesson. Use AI to write frames at three levels, check they ask for the same thinking, and add a word bank.
You can now write sentence frames that support every English level in the same task.

options: A structure for a response with blanks to fill
check.why: Frames show students how to build a response.

check.q: Your beginning-level frame asks students to name a color, while the advanced one asks them to explain a cause. What would you change?
options: Make every level ask for the same thinking with different support
check.why: Frames at every level ask for the same thinking; only the support changes.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: A translation workflow with human checks
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Set a four-step workflow for translating family communications.
This lesson builds toward: Given a family message, you will run a four-step translation workflow: plain English, approved tool, qualified check, save, sending nothing until a qualified speaker has checked it.
AI translation is fast and often good, but it makes mistakes that matter: wrong dates, wrong tone, school terms with no direct translation, and errors in less widely used languages. Families rely on what the school sends them.
A four-step workflow: 1) Write the English in plain language first (short sentences, no idioms or jargon); clear English translates better. 2) Translate with an approved tool. 3) A qualified speaker (district translator, bilingual staff member or contracted service) checks and corrects it. 4) Send, and keep the checked version for reuse.
For high-stakes communication (special education, discipline, health and safety, legal rights), use professional translation or interpretation as your district requires. Do not ask students to translate for their own families on important matters.
Step by step:
- Write plain English first: no idioms or jargon.
- Translate with an approved tool.
- A qualified speaker checks and corrects.
- Send, and save the checked version.
- High-stakes messages: professional translation or interpretation.
Words to know:
- Idiom: a phrase whose meaning is not the sum of its words, like "touch base".
- Interpretation: translating spoken language, for example at a meeting.
Try it now: Write a short family message about a school event in plain English, translate it with an approved tool, and ask a qualified speaker to check it. Record each correction.
You can now run a translation workflow where a qualified person checks every AI translation.

check.q: Why write the message in plain English before translating it?
options: Plain English is shorter to print
Translation tools only read plain English
check.why: Clear source text leads to fewer translation errors.

check.q: A teacher wants a student to translate a note about the student's own grades for their parents. What would you suggest?
options: Use AI and send it without a check
Use the workflow with a qualified speaker's check instead
check.why: Students should not translate important matters for their own families.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Obligations, privacy and current guidance
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Identify who confirms your school's obligations to multilingual families and where to check current guidance.
This lesson builds toward: When questions come up about obligations to multilingual families, you will identify who in your district confirms current obligations and describe student needs to AI only in general terms, with their contact written on your workflow page.
Schools have long had federal civil-rights obligations to English learners and to communicate with parents who have limited English proficiency in a language they understand. In August 2025, as reported by K-12 Dive, the US Department of Education rescinded its 2015 joint Dear Colleague Letter on English learners, saying it did not align with the administration's priorities. Dear Colleague letters are guidance, not law.
Because guidance has changed, do not rely on old summaries. Ask your district's English learner office, civil-rights or Title VI coordinator, or counsel what your current obligations are, and check your state education agency's English learner guidance, which may set its own requirements.
Privacy still applies: a student's English learner status, language background and proficiency scores are part of education records protected by FERPA. Keep them out of unapproved AI tools, and describe needs in general terms when you prompt.
Step by step:
- Do not rely on old summaries of EL guidance.
- Ask your district EL office or civil-rights coordinator about current obligations.
- Check your state education agency's EL guidance.
- Keep EL status and scores out of unapproved AI tools.
- Prompt with general descriptions of needs.
Words to know:
- English learner (EL): a student identified as needing support to learn English for school.
- Limited English proficiency (LEP): not yet able to read, write, speak or understand English well enough for a situation.
- Rescind: to cancel or withdraw an earlier guidance or decision.
Official sources:
- K-12 Dive: Education Department rescinds English learner guidance (Aug 2025)
- FERPA: Protecting Student Privacy
Try it now: Find out who in your district answers questions about communication with multilingual families (EL office, civil-rights coordinator or family liaison) and write their contact on your workflow page.
You can now find your current obligations to multilingual families and keep their information private.

check.why: Dear Colleague letters explain how agencies read the law; they are guidance.

check.q: You are unsure what your school must provide in translated communication. Who do you ask?
options: Your district EL office or civil-rights coordinator
check.why: District EL and civil-rights staff know your current obligations.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Leading with home languages as a strength
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Plan how your school will use AI to value home languages, not replace people.
This lesson builds toward: For your school, you will plan how AI will support home languages without replacing bilingual staff, with one measure of better family communication.
AI translation can make it seem as if bilingual staff and interpreters are less needed. The opposite is true: AI drafts make their checks faster, and their knowledge of culture and community cannot be automated. Protect their time for the checks and for the conversations that matter most.
Use AI to honor home languages: let students explain ideas in their home language first and then build the English, create glossaries and welcome materials in families' languages, and invite families to share knowledge. Avoid tools or rules that treat home languages only as a problem.
Bring it together in a short school plan: which supports teachers will use, the translation workflow, who checks, how families give feedback, and how you will know families are better informed (for example, attendance at events or a short survey in their languages).
Step by step:
- Protect bilingual staff time for checks and key conversations.
- Let students use home languages to build ideas.
- Create welcome materials in families' languages.
- Write a short school plan with the workflow and checkers.
- Measure whether families are better informed.
Words to know:
- Asset-based: seeing what students and families bring as strengths, not deficits.
- Family liaison: a staff member who builds connections between school and families.
Try it now: Final task: build your multilingual support pack (adapted text, checked bilingual glossary, three-level sentence frames, one checked family translation), write your four-step translation workflow with the checker's contact, and note every correction made.
You can now lead AI use that supports multilingual learners and families accurately and respectfully.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Adapted text Key ideas were lost or simplified away. An adapted version that keeps the grade-level ideas. Passes the same-questions test and keeps academic vocabulary with support. Bilingual glossary Fewer than 8 words, or not checked by a qualified speaker. 8 to 10 key words in one home language, checked by a qualified speaker. Cognates and false friends are marked, with an example for each word. Sentence frames Fewer than three levels, or levels ask for different thinking. Frames at three proficiency levels for the lesson's main task. Every level asks for the same thinking, and beginning frames include a word bank. Checked family translation The translation was not checked by a qualified speaker. One family message translated by AI and checked by a qualified speaker, with corrections noted. The checked version is saved for reuse. Translation workflow Fewer than four steps, or no checker contact. A four-step workflow your school will follow. Includes the checker's contact and who to ask about obligations. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What does asset-based mean for multilingual learners?
options: Seeing what students bring as strengths
check.why: An asset-based view treats home languages as strengths.

check.q: A leader suggests AI translation means bilingual staff are no longer needed. What would you say?
options: Suggest replacing family liaisons with chatbots
Their checks get faster, and their community knowledge still matters
check.why: AI speeds the work, but qualified people check it and know the community.
